books.title: I'd Like To Be
books.art_why: The book shows real-world jobs and everyday settings, so photographs suit it.

pages.text: I’d like to be a cook and make a dish with meats and sweets and veggies and fish. I’d learn to cook, not by the book but by testing, tasting, and taking a look.
pages.brief: A cook makes a dish with meats, sweets, vegetables and fish. The cook learns to cook not by the book but by carefully testing the food, tasting it and taking a look at the dish.

pages.text: See my kitchen? Come and pitch in! My stew ’s alive with corn and chives.
pages.brief: A smiling child stands in a kitchen and invites someone to come and pitch in. A pot of stew is alive with corn and chives, and the child proudly shows the warm, busy cooking space.

pages.text: I’d like to be a maker of video games full of dragons and wizards with crazy names. The game I’d write would who run and jump and get in fights.
pages.brief: A busy video game maker creates a game full of dragons and wizards with crazy names. On a screen, the exciting game being written shows fantasy characters who run and jump and get in fights.

pages.text: This game is a fun fantasy. I’d like it if you played with me!
pages.brief: A smiling child shares a fun fantasy game and asks someone nearby to play along. The game world is full of colorful, imaginative fun, and the child eagerly invites a playmate into the exciting fantasy.

pages.text: I’d like to gaze into the sky, and take notes on what’s passing by. I’d search for planets near and far. I’d help to name each brand new star.
pages.brief: An astronomer gazes into the night sky and carefully takes notes on what is passing by high above. The astronomer searches for planets both near and far and helps name each bright, brand new star.

pages.text: I would help discover things, from galaxies to Saturn’s rings.
pages.brief: A scientist studies the wide, far sky and helps discover things from galaxies to Saturn's rings. Looking out into deep space, the scientist finds these wonders and shares the discoveries proudly with care and wonder.

pages.text: I’d like to be a vet who helps sick cats, and barking dogs and hurting bats. People would bring their pets to me. I would help them stay healthy.
pages.brief: A caring vet in a busy clinic calmly helps sick cats, barking dogs and hurting bats. People bring all their pets to the vet, who gently checks them with care and helps them stay healthy.

pages.text: I’d heal their cuts and fix their legs, and help with birds who lay bad eggs.
pages.brief: At a busy clinic, a caring vet gently heals cuts and fixes legs and helps birds who lay bad eggs. The vet gives careful care to all kinds of animals with injuries and egg troubles.

pages.text: I’d like to be an artist for comic books. I’d draw superheroes and pirate’s hooks and evil people who’d destroy man or woman, girl or boy.
pages.brief: A busy comic book artist at a desk carefully draws all superheroes, pirate's hooks and evil people who would destroy man or woman, girl or boy. The artist works on many comic book pages with care.

pages.text: Their plots won’t make it off the ground— not with Super Boy around.
pages.brief: Super Boy appears boldly in the comic, stopping the evil plots from getting off the ground. The comic book artist shows Super Boy defeating the plots on the page and keeping them from taking off.

pages.text: I’d like to fix cool cars in an auto shop. I’d get them going when they stop. I’d do repairs and make them run. That is my idea of fun.
pages.brief: In a busy auto shop, a cheerful worker carefully fixes all the cool cars. The worker proudly gets them going when they stop, doing repairs with skill and care and making them run again safely.

pages.text: I’d fix their engines when they stall. Getting greasy is a ball!
pages.brief: In the busy auto shop, the cheerful worker fixes all the engines when they stall. Getting greasy is part of the fun as the worker cheerfully repairs the engines with tools and a big smile.

pages.text: Life has endless possibilities. What in the world would you like to be?
pages.brief: A child stands with an open, wondering look, thinking about life's endless possibilities. The child spreads their arms wide and cheerfully asks a nearby young friend what in the world they would like to be.

books.title: Summer Olympic Events
books.art_why: Modern Summer Olympics and athletes are real, photographable subjects.

pages.text: Summer Olympics Host Cities The Summer Olympic Games The Summer Olympics are held every four years. They are held in different cities around the world.
pages.brief: A wide view of different host cities around the world shows the Summer Olympic Games taking place every four years. City buildings in each host city make clear that the Games are held in different cities around the world.

pages.text: Athletes at the Games compete to win medals for their countries. They participate in hundreds of events. Let’s look at some events.
pages.brief: Athletes from different countries compete at the Games, working to win medals for their countries. The scene shows a busy Games setting with hundreds of events, as many athletes take part and try to win medals in their sports.

pages.text: Water Sports One water sport is swimming. Some swimming races are short, and swimmers swim only two lengths of the pool. Other races are longer.
pages.brief: Swimmers race in a pool during water sports events. Some races are short, with swimmers swimming only two lengths of the pool, while other swimming races are longer and show swimmers racing over more lengths.

pages.text: Some swimming races use only one kind of stroke. In one race, swimmers can choose the type of stroke they want to use.
pages.brief: In a pool, swimmers race using only one kind of stroke in some swimming races during competition. In one race, swimmers choose the type of stroke they want to use as they swim across the pool.

pages.text: Diving is another water sport. In diving events, divers jump from high above the water, and they twist, flip and turn while in the air. They get points for how well they dive.
pages.brief: Divers jump from high above the water in diving events. While in the air, divers twist, flip and turn, then enter the water. They receive points for how well they dive, with the divers shown high above the pool.

pages.text: Track and Field Track and field events include running, throwing, and jumping competitions. The marathon is the longest running event, and the shortest races are called dashes.
pages.brief: Track and field events show running, throwing and jumping competitions. Marathon runners run the longest running event, while short races called dashes show the shortest running event. Athletes are seen running, throwing and jumping at the track and field setting.

pages.text: In throwing events, athletes throw objects as far as they can. People competing in these events must be very strong.
pages.brief: Strong athletes take part in throwing events, throwing objects as far as they can. The scene shows people competing in these events, using their strength and powerful body movements to throw objects far at the Games.

pages.text: In jumping events, athletes jump high or far. In the high jump, athletes leap over a bar. The bar is raised higher and higher until only one person can jump it. In the long jump, athletes leap as far as they can.
pages.brief: In jumping events, athletes jump high or far. A high jumper leaps over a bar that is raised higher and higher until only one person can jump it. Nearby, a long jumper leaps as far as they can in the long jump.

pages.text: Gymnastics Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl through the air. They need strength, skill, and perfect timing.
pages.brief: Gymnasts leap, flip and twirl through the air in gymnastics events. They show strength, skill and perfect timing as they move through the air during the event, with gymnasts performing athletic moves in a gymnastics setting.

pages.text: One event is the balance beam. Gymnasts must balance on the beam while they turn and flip.
pages.brief: A gymnast balances on the balance beam during a gymnastics event. While on the beam, the gymnast turns and flips, keeping balance on the narrow beam and showing skill in the gymnastics setting.

pages.text: Another event is the rings. Gymnasts hold onto the rings and flip their bodies in circles.
pages.brief: A gymnast holds onto the rings in a gymnastics event. While holding the rings, the gymnast flips their body in circles, using strength and control and showing skill on the rings in the gymnastics setting.

pages.text: Event Categories The Summer Olympics include many sports with hundreds of events. Which events do you like? Summer Olympic Sports.
pages.brief: Many Summer Olympic sports and hundreds of events are shown together. Athletes take part in different event categories across the Games, giving a wide view of the many sports and events in the Summer Olympics.

books.title: Ships and Boats
books.art_why: Real ships, boats, and waterways exist and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Ships and boats are part of our history. Before cars, trains, or airplanes, they were the fastest way to travel. Even today, they continue to get bigger and faster.
pages.brief: A large modern ship and a smaller boat move across open water. The big ship is sleek and fast, showing how ships and boats have grown bigger and quicker than the boats of long ago.

pages.text: Early Ships and Boats The first boats were dugout canoes. They were made from just one log. They were used in rivers, lakes, and oceans around the world. People used poles to push some of these boats.
pages.brief: A dugout canoe made from one single log floats on a river. A person stands in it and pushes with a long pole, moving the simple boat through the water as people did long ago.

pages.text: Other boats used paddles or oars. These are long pieces of wood with wide, flat ends. They pushed against the water to move the boat ahead. Later, people made boats with wooden frames. They covered the frames with bark, reeds, skins.
pages.brief: A wooden boat moves across the water while a person pulls long oars with wide, flat ends. The oars push against the water. Nearby, another boat shows a wooden frame covered with bark, reeds, and skins.

pages.text: Some people built boats that could sail well beyond the islands where they lived. They took two canoes and joined them with large wooden poles. This kind of boat was called a catamaran. These boats could travel very fast. They also allowed safe travel from one island to another.
pages.brief: A catamaran sails quickly over the ocean between islands. It is made of two canoes joined together with large wooden poles, and it moves fast and safely across the water. People built it to travel beyond their island homes.

pages.text: Some frame than log boats. Many people at the same time. These ships were called galleys. At times they carried hundreds of rowers.
pages.brief: A large galley ship moves across the water. Many rowers sit in rows and pull long oars, while the big ship carries hundreds of people at the same time. It is a busy scene with many oars in the water.

pages.text: Sails made from strong cloth were also used to move boats. The sails caught the wind. The wind pushed the boat. As ships became bigger, they needed more sails. Sailing ships carried explorers all around the world.
pages.brief: A sailing ship with large cloth sails moves across the open ocean. The wind catches the sails and pushes the boat forward on its long journey around the world. More sails help the bigger ship travel.

pages.text: Modern Ships and Boats Today, many boats are made of metal and plastic. Many ships and boats use electricity to turn propellers. The propellers push the boat through the water. Boats with propellers are everywhere.
pages.brief: A modern boat made of metal and plastic moves through the water. Under the boat, a propeller turns with electricity and pushes the boat ahead, showing how common propeller boats are today. This is a common sight on the water.

pages.text: Cruise ships are like floating hotels. They can carry thousands of people. Huge tankers carry oil and gas over the ocean.
pages.brief: A huge cruise ship floats on the ocean like a floating hotel, carrying thousands of people. Nearby, a very large tanker ship carries oil and gas across the water. Both ships are enormous and travel far over the sea.

pages.text: Tugboats push and pull larger ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people. Fireboats put out fires on other ships.
pages.brief: A tugboat pushes a larger ship through the water. A ferryboat carries cars and people across, and a fireboat sprays water onto a fire on another ship. These working boats help other ships and people on the water.

pages.text: Many countries use ships and boats, large and small, to defend their coasts. Submarines move under the water. Planes and helicopters take off and land on aircraft carriers.
pages.brief: A submarine moves under the water near a coast. Above, an aircraft carrier has a plane and a helicopter ready to take off and land, while ships and boats defend the coast. Many countries use these to guard their shores.

pages.text: People still use smaller boats for fishing, fun, and sport. Many of these boats still use paddles or oars.
pages.brief: A small boat floats on a lake while a person uses paddles or oars to move it. The boat is used for fishing, fun, and sport. People still use these small boats today.

pages.text: Conclusion Ships and boats have changed a lot over the years. Even so, they are still an important way to move quickly over the water.
pages.brief: An old wooden boat and a modern fast boat move over the water side by side. Ships and boats have changed a lot over the years, but they still carry people quickly across the water.

books.title: Where's the Joey?
books.art_why: Real marsupials, joeys, and habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: What’s a Joey? A joey is a baby marsupial (mar-SOO-pee-ul). A marsupial is an unusual type of animal. Its babies are carried in a pouch, or pocket, on the mother’s belly. As it grows, the little joey stays hidden inside the pouch.
pages.brief: A mother marsupial stands with a tiny baby joey tucked inside the pouch on her belly. The little joey is hidden and small as it grows inside the pouch. It stays close to the mother’s body.

pages.text: Safe inside, the tiny joey drinks milk and grows while it is carried around. Even after it can walk, the joey may still ride in mom’s pouch.
pages.brief: A mother marsupial carries a tiny joey in her pouch. Inside, the joey drinks milk and grows while the mother moves around. Even after it can walk, the joey may still ride in mom’s pouch.

pages.text: There are over three hundred types of marsupials. Most of them live in Australia (aw-STRAYL-yuh) and eat plants. Let’s look at a few kinds of marsupials and their joeys.
pages.brief: Several different marsupials are shown together in a peaceful Australian setting. Most of them are quietly eating plants. The group shows just a few of the over three hundred types of marsupials that live there.

pages.text: A Jumping Joey This joey stays in its mother’s pouch for eight months while it grows very tall. Its feet and tail grow very long, too. Can you guess what it is?
pages.brief: A joey with very long feet and a long tail is tucked in its mother’s pouch. It stays inside for eight months while it grows very tall, and its feet and tail grow very long, too.

pages.text: It’s a red kangaroo! A red kangaroo is the largest marsupial. It can stand over six feet tall and weigh 200 lbs (91 kg). It can jump 30 feet (9 m) with each leap!
pages.brief: A red kangaroo stands tall on strong hind legs in an open space. It is the largest marsupial, with a big body that can weigh 200 pounds. It leaps through the air, jumping far with each bound.

pages.text: A Joey That Lives in a Tree When grown, this little joey will look like a furry teddy bear with big ears. It will live most of its life sitting in trees and eating leaves. Can you guess what it is?
pages.brief: A little joey with big ears sits in a tree, eating leaves. When grown, it will look like a furry teddy bear with big ears. It will spend most of its life sitting in trees and eating leaves.

pages.text: It’s a koala! A koala lives, eats, and sleeps in eucalyptus (yoo-kuh-LIP-tus) trees. It is happy just to sit and eat lots of leaves every day. A koala usually only walks around at night.
pages.brief: A koala sits in a eucalyptus tree, eating lots of leaves. Another koala sleeps quietly among the branches. A koala usually walks around only at night, so one is shown moving nearby in the dark.

pages.text: Joey the Screamer This marsupial mom might carry three or four noisy joeys in her pouch at one time. Her little joeys can scream very loudly. What are they?
pages.brief: A marsupial mother stands with three or four little joeys in her pouch. The joeys have their mouths wide open and look very noisy as they scream loudly. The mother carries the noisy group together.

pages.text: They are Tasmanian devils! The Tasmanian devil gets its name from its loud screams, sharp teeth, bad smell, and wild look. It is a meat-eater, and lives only on the island of Tasmania (taz-MAY-nee-uh).
pages.brief: A Tasmanian devil with a wild look and sharp teeth screams very loudly. It has a bad smell and a fierce appearance. The meat-eater is shown eating and lives only on the island of Tasmania.

pages.text: Do You Know?
pages.brief: A simple scene shows a marsupial mother standing quietly with her joey safe in her pouch. The pair is calm and close together, and the gentle picture invites a moment to think about what the reader knows.

pages.text: Protecting the Marsupials Most marsupials eat plants, and many, like the koala, live quietly in forests. When those forests are cut down, their homes, food, and safety are lost. Other marsupials have lost their sources of food to herds of grazing cows or growing cities.
pages.brief: A koala sits quietly in a forest tree while trees nearby are being cut down. Cows graze in a field, and a growing city spreads close to the forest. Marsupials lose their homes, food, and safety.

pages.text: Marsupials Are Special Animals Most marsupials and their joeys live in only one place on Earth. We need to protect their special habitats and food sources—so we will always know where the joeys are. Learn More About Marsupials.
pages.brief: A mother marsupial and her joey sit together in their special habitat, with plants and trees around them. A view of Earth shows that most marsupials and joeys live in only one place on the planet.

books.title: Día de los Muertos
books.art_why: A present-day cultural holiday celebrated by real families in Mexico and the United States, so real photographs exist.

pages.text: When and Where? People all over the world celebrate Día de los Muertos, or “Day of the Dead.” People in Mexico have celebrated holidays like this one for thousands of years. All over the United States, people hold parades and celebrations. These usually take place around November 1 and 2.
pages.brief: A crowded street parade with families in colorful costumes and painted faces walking together, some holding marigold flowers. In the background, a Mexican town square with banners and a church, and further off a United States city street with a similar parade, showing celebrations in both countries.

pages.text: Is It Halloween? Día de los Muertos might seem like Halloween. The two holidays are different, though. Halloween is often about scaring people. Día de los Muertos is a time of joy. People remember and celebrate loved ones who have died.
pages.brief: A split scene: on one side a cheerful family gathering with flowers, candles and smiling faces remembering loved ones; on the other side a darker, spooky doorway. The bright, joyful side dominates, showing a happy family celebrating together.

pages.text: Lidia’s Día de los Muertos Lidia Terán-Cooper grew up in Mexico. Lidia and her family spent every Día de los Muertos at the cemetery. The family brought flowers and a picnic.
pages.brief: A young girl, Lidia, standing with her family among gravestones in a Mexican cemetery. The family spreads a picnic blanket on the ground, sets down baskets of flowers and food, and settles in together for the day beside the graves.

pages.text: They told stories about those who had died. Bands played special songs. Lidia and the other children danced and played all day. Día de los Muertos was always a happy day for Lidia.
pages.brief: Families seated around picnic blankets in the cemetery, an older relative telling a story with hands moving. Nearby a small band plays guitars and trumpets while children in their best clothes dance and chase each other between the graves, laughing.

pages.text: Lidia lives in the United States now. Lidia and her family walk in the parade in Tucson (TOO-sawn), Arizona, every year.
pages.brief: Lidia, now an adult, walking down a sunlit street in Tucson, Arizona, with her family in a Day of the Dead parade. Dancers, musicians and costumed marchers surround them as onlookers line the sidewalks and cheer.

pages.text: Before the parade, Lidia makes masks. Children and adults paint the masks and wear them in the parade.
pages.brief: Lidia at a table covered with plain white masks, brushes and pots of bright paint. Children and adults on either side of her paint the masks in vivid colors and hold finished ones up to their faces, ready for the parade.

pages.text: Day of the Dead for Children Some places have a parade for children. Children decorate cardboard wings to wear. They paint their faces and put on costumes.
pages.brief: A parade just for children moving along a street. Kids wear painted faces, costumes and large cardboard wings decorated with bright patterns on their backs, walking and waving while grown-ups watch from the side.

pages.text: Altars Día de los Muertos has many other traditions. Some people build altars in their homes. The altars are covered with cloth. The family puts up photos of the person who has died. They might add a favorite item or piece of clothing of the loved one.
pages.brief: Inside a home, a table set up as an altar and draped with cloth. A family places a framed photograph of a smiling woman at the center and adds a folded sweater and a small favorite object beside it.

pages.text: The family lights candles around the altars. They also make special bread. They might even leave a favorite drink. Flowers, skeleton toys, and dolls also decorate the altars.
pages.brief: The finished altar glowing with lit candles, marigold flowers, a loaf of special bread and a cup of drink. Small skeleton toys and dolls sit among the flowers, and family members stand before it looking at the photo.

pages.text: Sugar Skulls Some people make sugar skulls. People decorate the sugar skulls with colorful frosting. Children love eating the sweet skulls.
pages.brief: Hands decorating white sugar skulls with swirling lines of colorful frosting in pink, blue and yellow. A group of children at a table hold the finished skulls and bite into the sweet ones, grinning.

pages.text: Art Some artists make paintings for the holiday. The paintings show skeletons dancing and playing music. The art is a way to celebrate friends and family members who have died.
pages.brief: An artist in a studio painting a canvas of dancing skeletons playing guitars and trumpets. Finished paintings lean against the wall, and a small group of visitors looks at the dancing skeleton figures.

pages.text: Full of Life Día de los Muertos helps people to feel better after losing someone they love. Marching in a parade or decorating altars can help them celebrate that special person. No other holiday is so full of life, costumes, masks, joy, memories, and love.
pages.brief: A wide street parade scene with marching families in masks and costumes, mixed with an altar at the edge of the frame holding candles, flowers and photographs. People smile and hold hands, celebrating together in a bright and joyful crowd.

books.title: Tarantula!
books.art_why: Real tarantulas and their natural habitats exist today, so photographs suit this nature book.

pages.text: Introduction What’s huge and hairy, and has fangs that can kill? It’s the biggest spider in the world—the tarantula! Do You Know?
pages.brief: A huge, hairy tarantula fills the frame, showing its fangs prominently. It is the biggest spider in the world. The spider looks powerful and threatening, and no people or other animals appear around it. The image focuses closely on the spider alone.

pages.text: Where Tarantulas Live Tarantulas live in warm places around the world. Many live in forests, and others live in deserts. More than fifty kinds of tarantulas live in the United States. Some tarantulas live in holes in the ground. Others live under logs or in trees. Do You Know?
pages.brief: Several tarantulas are shown in warm places around the world. One tarantula stands in a forest, another in a desert, and others near holes in the ground, under a log, and in a tree. More than fifty kinds live in the United States.

pages.text: Hard, Hairy Bodies Like insects and other spiders, tarantulas have a hard covering on their body. As they grow, the covering gets too tight and splits down the middle. After a tarantula pushes out of the old skin, its new skin gets hard.
pages.brief: A tarantula is shown with a hard covering on its body. The covering has split down the middle as the spider grows. The tarantula pushes out of the old skin, and its new skin appears ready to harden.

pages.text: A tarantula is covered with hairs. The hairs sense heat, cold, and things that move. Other hairs near its mouth help a tarantula taste and smell. Stiff hairs with points grow on its stomach and back. A tarantula can sting enemies with these hairs.
pages.brief: A close view of a tarantula shows hairs covering its body. Hairs near its mouth are visible, and stiff, pointed hairs grow on its stomach and back. The spider’s hairs appear to sense heat, cold, and movement, and the stiff hairs can sting enemies.

pages.text: The legs of a tarantula have little claws with hairs. The hairs help the tarantula hold on when it climbs. Two little arms near its mouth have sharp parts. The tarantula holds and cuts food with them. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A tarantula is shown climbing, holding on with legs that have little claws and hairs. Near its mouth, two little arms with sharp parts are visible. The tarantula uses these arms to hold and cut food.

pages.text: Do You Know?
pages.brief: A single tarantula is shown alone in a plain, neutral view. No action, setting, people, or other animals appear. The image stays simple and uncluttered, focusing only on the spider itself without adding anything else.

pages.text: Eating and Being Eaten Tarantulas rest during the day and come out at night to hunt. They eat insects, frogs, lizards, bats, mice, and small snakes. They also eat spiders—even other tarantulas.
pages.brief: A tarantula rests during the day, then comes out at night to hunt. It is shown with insects, a frog, a lizard, a bat, a mouse, and a small snake nearby. Another spider, even another tarantula, is also shown as possible prey.

pages.text: To catch prey, a tarantula sits very still and waits. When an animal comes near, the tarantula jumps and jabs its fangs into it. Venom shoots into the animal and makes it stop moving.
pages.brief: A tarantula sits very still and waits for prey. When an animal comes near, the tarantula jumps and jabs its fangs into it. Venom shoots into the animal, and the animal stops moving. The action is shown close and fast.

pages.text: The tarantula drags the animal back home. It uses its jaws and little arms to cut up the animal. It spits juices onto the pieces, which turn to mush. Then the tarantula sucks up a tasty meal. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A tarantula drags a caught animal back to its home. It uses its jaws and little arms to cut the animal into pieces. It spits juices onto the pieces, which turn to mush, then the tarantula sucks up the meal.

pages.text: You might think tarantulas are too big to be hunted. Not true! The tarantula hawk—a big wasp—hunts tarantulas as food for its young. A female wasp stings a tarantula, which then stops moving. The wasp lays one egg on the tarantula’s body. When the young insect comes out, it feeds on the tarantula.
pages.brief: A big wasp called a tarantula hawk is shown hunting a tarantula. The female wasp stings the tarantula until it stops moving, then lays one egg on the tarantula’s body. When the young insect comes out, it feeds on the tarantula.

pages.text: How Safe Are Tarantulas? Many people are scared of tarantulas because they are so big. Tarantulas are harmless if you leave them alone. Some tarantulas are slow and calm. Others are fast and looking for a fight, so don’t mess with them! Do You Know?
pages.brief: People are shown keeping a safe distance from tarantulas because the spiders are so big. One tarantula looks slow and calm, while another looks fast and ready to fight. The people leave them alone instead of bothering them.

pages.text: Do You Know? People are a bigger danger to tarantulas than any other threat. These amazing spiders are important to the balance of nature. They deserve to be protected.
pages.brief: People are shown as a bigger danger to tarantulas than any other threat. A tarantula stands in a natural setting that shows its importance to the balance of nature. The scene suggests these amazing spiders deserve protection and care.

books.title: Strange Plants
books.art_why: Real plants and natural habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: When we think about plants, we often think of trees, flowers, and grass. Like most plants, these plants have green leaves. They also have roots growing into the ground.
pages.brief: A group of ordinary plants is shown together: leafy trees, flowers, and low grass. Each plant has green leaves, and below the ground their roots reach down into the soil. The scene shows the familiar parts of most plants in a natural outdoor setting.

pages.text: Some plants are not like most plants. This book is about some of these strange plants.
pages.brief: Several unusual plants are shown growing in a natural setting, standing apart from the familiar trees, flowers, and grass. Their shapes and leaves look different from most plants, hinting at strange plants.

pages.text: Plants called air plants live in trees high above the ground. Their roots are not buried in dirt. Instead, they grow on tree branches. They take moisture from the air, not from the soil as most plants do.
pages.brief: Air plants grow high above the ground on tree branches, not buried in dirt. Their roots cling to the branch instead of reaching into soil. Around them, moisture in the air touches their leaves. The scene shows the tree canopy where these plants live.

pages.text: Can you imagine plants that eat meat? Well, there are such plants. They eat insects, spiders, and even some other small animals. One well-known meat-eating plant is the Venus flytrap.
pages.brief: A Venus flytrap is shown among other meat-eating plants. Small insects, a spider, and a tiny animal are nearby. The plant's leaves are open and ready, showing how some plants catch and eat small creatures instead of getting food only from soil.

pages.text: Its leaves look like traps. They have small spikes along their edges. When a critter walks inside a leaf, the leaf snaps shut. The critter is trapped.
pages.brief: Close view of a Venus flytrap leaf shaped like a trap, with small spikes along its edges. A small critter has walked inside the leaf, and the leaf is snapping shut around it. The critter is caught inside the closed trap.

pages.text: The sundew is also a meat-eating plant. It has many sticky hairs on its surface. Insects landing on it get stuck. Then the plant digests the insects. The giant sundew plant of Australia even eats small frogs!
pages.brief: A sundew plant is shown with many sticky hairs on its surface. Small insects have landed and are stuck to the hairs. Nearby, a giant sundew in Australia is shown with a small frog, because this kind of sundew can eat small frogs.

pages.text: Some plants steal food from other plants. The dodder plant sends rootlike parts into another plant. It sucks food and water from the plant. It is a parasite. A parasite lives off another living thing.
pages.brief: A dodder plant is shown attached to another plant. Rootlike parts from the dodder reach into the host plant and draw food and water from it. The host plant stands beside the dodder, showing how this parasite lives off another living plant.

pages.text: Many flowers have bad smells that attract insects. The stapelia flower smells like rotting meat. Flies like the smell, so they fly into the flower. Special powder gets on their bodies. They take the powder to other flowers. The flowers use the powder to make seeds and grow new plants.
pages.brief: A stapelia flower is shown with flies landing on it. The flower is shown as flies are drawn to its rotting-meat smell. Special powder sticks to the flies' bodies as they visit. The flies then carry the powder to other flowers, helping the plants make seeds.

pages.text: Some plants look like stones. The plants in this picture are called “stone plants” or “living stones.” They live in very hot, dry places. They hold water very well. Their shape helps to hide them so that animals do not eat them.

pages.text: Snail The animal world has some very slow animals in it. One of the very slowest is the snail. Even the fastest snails are pretty slow. In 1995, Archie the snail took two minutes and twenty seconds to crawl 13 inches (33 cm).
pages.brief: A small snail named Archie crawls slowly across bare ground, its shell tilted as it stretches forward. Its soft body and tiny tentacles are close enough to see. Around it is open, quiet ground, with nothing rushed or busy, showing one of the slowest animals in the world.

pages.text: Starfish Snails aren’t the only slow animals. Starfish don’t seem to move at all. At top speed, they just creep along. A starfish needs four minutes to move the length of a man’s arm.
pages.brief: A starfish rests on the sandy sea floor, its arms spread as it creeps almost imperceptibly forward. The water is calm and clear, and the starfish seems barely to move at all. The scene focuses only on the starfish and the slow, creeping motion described.

pages.text: Three-toed Sloth The three-toed sloth hangs around in trees most of the time. Because it seldom moves, little plants often grow on its fur. A sloth needs about three minutes to crawl the length of two cars.

books.title: Model Rockets
books.art_why: Model rockets, kits, launches and clubs are real modern subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: A father and daughter work together to build a large model rocket.
pages.brief: A father and daughter work together at a table indoors to build a large model rocket, carefully assembling model rocket parts with tools around them as they fit the pieces of the big rocket together.

pages.text: Liftoff! Three... two... one... liftoff! rocket shoots into the sky. The rocket can fly up to 1,500 feet (457 m) high! Watching these small rockets fly can be fun and exciting. Model rockets aren’t just for fun, though. They also teach us about science and space.
pages.brief: A model rocket launches into the sky after a countdown, shooting far up as high as 1,500 feet; people watch the small rocket fly, finding it fun and exciting while learning about science and space.

pages.text: Kids have been building and painting model rockets for decades. The History of Rockets People in China invented rockets about eight hundred years ago. They filled tubes with gunpowder and shot them at their enemies. Later, scientists built rockets that could go into space. Starting in the 1950s, people began building model rockets for fun. Model Rockets.
pages.brief: People in China fill tubes with gunpowder and shoot them at enemies about eight hundred years ago; later scientists build rockets that go into space, and from the 1950s people begin building model rockets for fun.

pages.text: The pieces of a model rocket need to be carefully put together (top). A finished rocket is ready to fly (bottom). Parts of a Model Rocket A model rocket kit comes with all the parts a rocket needs.
pages.brief: A model rocket kit’s pieces are laid out and carefully put together on a table, showing all the parts a rocket needs; nearby, a finished model rocket stands complete on display and ready to fly.

pages.text: Nose cones and rocket bodies come in many shapes and sizes. A model rocket’s body is a long tube made of cardboard or plastic. The nose cone fits into the top of the tube. The size and shape of a rocket’s body and nose cone can change how it flies. Model Rockets.
pages.brief: Several model rocket nose cones and body tubes appear in many shapes and sizes; a long cardboard or plastic tube has a nose cone fitted into its top, showing how body and nose cone shape can change flight.

pages.text: At the Launchpad The only place to launch a rocket is in an open space. The launch area needs to be far away from people and buildings. A large field or a playground is a good spot. pages.text: Even in a large launch area, a rocket can get stuck in a tree as it floats back to the ground on its parachute. If a rocket gets stuck in a tall tree or on a power line, it should be left there for safety reasons. Model rockets are fun, but they can be dangerous. Follow these rules to stay safe: • Use only safe materials and engines in your rocket. • Always launch your rocket outside in an open area. • Make sure there is no dry grass or any other fire hazard at the launch site. • Make sure everyone is at least 15 feet (4.5 m) away before you launch your rocket. • Count down before you launch. • Ask an adult for help if you have any questions. Model Rockets.
pages.brief: A model rocket floats down on its parachute and gets stuck in a tall tree; the launch area is open, and people stay back for safety, leaving the rocket where it is rather than reaching near a power line.

pages.text: A Cub Scout launches a model rocket in Boston. Clubs and Competitions People who fly model rockets often join model rocket clubs. Schools or groups can have information about model rocket clubs. A science center or museum might have a model rocket club, too.
