books.title: The Mighty Mississippi
books.art_why: The Mississippi River, its wildlife, boats, cities and floods are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: A Long Journey Rain falls on Lake Itasca. It mixes into the clear waters of a river so small that a child could wade across Mississippi it. So begins the mighty River. A Lake of Many Names.
pages.brief: Rain falls on Lake Itasca, mixing into clear water that becomes a very small river. Show the lake surface, falling raindrops, and a narrow stream winding between green shores, shallow enough for a child to wade across.

pages.text: Over the next three months, the water will take a 2,350-mile (3,781 km) journey through ten U.S. states. At last, it will reach the Gulf of Mexico.
pages.brief: Show the river winding a long way across ten stretches of land, from small northern waters toward the Gulf of Mexico. The water travels 2,350 miles over three months, passing through varied country before reaching the sea.

pages.text: The Upper River At first, the river flows through dozens of locks and dams. They work together to raise or lower the water around boats. The water levels change to allow boats to travel safely. They also hold back water so boats don’t hit the river bottom.
pages.brief: Show the upper river flowing through locks and dams, with a boat inside a lock. Water levels rise or lower around the boat so it can travel safely, and the dams hold back water to keep boats from hitting the river bottom.

pages.text: Boats on this part of the river carry corn and soybeans south. Much of this food is shipped around the world.
pages.brief: Show a river barge loaded with corn and soybeans moving south on the upper river. Nearby fields and a working boat show that much of this food is carried down the river and shipped around the world.

pages.text: More than fifty kinds of mammals live along the upper river. River otters love to play here. Oldies but Goodies.
pages.brief: Show river otters playing along the bank of the upper river. More than fifty kinds of mammals live along this stretch, and the otters tumble and splash playfully in the bright water near the shore.

pages.text: Farther down, a big, muddy river comes in from the west. It mixes with the clear waters of the Mississippi. The river grows brown and wide.
pages.brief: Show, farther down, a big, muddy river coming in from the west and mixing with the clear Mississippi. Where the two waters meet, the river grows brown and wide, spreading broadly across the surrounding landscape.

pages.text: For the next 190 miles (306 km), the river runs through areas with many wild animals. Bald eagles nest in the tall trees. They eat the fish that swim in the river.
pages.brief: Show a bald eagle nest in a tall tree beside the river. A bald eagle stands at the nest or carries a fish, while the river below runs through an area full of wild animals for the next 190 miles.

pages.text: The Lower River Another big river joins the Mississippi from the east. The river grows deep and even wider. In many spots, it stretches 1.5 miles (2.4 km) across.
pages.brief: Show another big river joining the Mississippi from the east. The combined river grows deep and even wider, stretching 1.5 miles across in many spots as it flows through the broad open lower river country.

pages.text: With so much water, the Mississippi is famous for its floods. They can cause a lot of damage, but not all floods are bad. Along the river’s banks, the floods leave behind rich soil for farming.
pages.brief: Show the Mississippi flooding over its banks, with floodwater spreading across nearby farmland. The flood leaves behind rich, dark soil on the fields along the river, good for farming even though floods can cause damage.

pages.text: More cities rise up here, and the boats carry iron, steel, rubber, and wood. They carry farm crops such as cotton from the area, too. Some things move north, back up the river, and some move farther south.
pages.brief: Show a busy city rising beside the wide lower river, with boats carrying iron, steel, rubber, wood, and cotton. Some cargo moves north back up the river, while some moves farther south toward the sea.

pages.text: Several types of turtles call this part of the river home. So do alligators! Swimming All Summer.
pages.brief: Show several turtles and alligators in this part of the river. Turtles rest near the water while alligators swim calmly nearby, living together in the lower Mississippi where several types of turtles make their home.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi Finally, the Mississippi flows into the Gulf of Mexico. The rain that fell in Lake Itasca three months ago has reached the sea. Someday, some of that water may return as rain to Lake Itasca. It may make the journey all over again. And again...
pages.brief: Show the wide Mississippi finally flowing into the Gulf of Mexico. Rain clouds gather in the distance, suggesting the water may someday return as rain to Lake Itasca and make the long journey all over again.

books.title: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing; the book includes 1800s history and underground cutaway views.

pages.text: Introduction Colorful pools and wild animals. Streams of hot water that shoot out of the ground. People can see these things and more at Yellowstone, which became the world’s first national park in 1872. National parks are areas of special, protected land.
pages.brief: A family stands on a boardwalk viewing a bright blue and orange hot spring while a geyser shoots steam nearby. Bison graze on the grassy plain beyond, showing the colorful pools, hot water streams, and wild animals of Yellowstone.

pages.text: A Hot Spot Many people who go to Yellowstone want to see Old Faithful geyser. A geyser is a hole in the ground that shoots steam and hot water into the air. Yellowstone has about three hundred of them. Old Faithful shoots water 100 feet (30 m) high about every ninety minutes. Yellowstone Supervolcano.
pages.brief: Old Faithful geyser erupts high into the air, sending a tall column of steam and hot water above a crowd of watching visitors. Other small geysers steam in the background across the rocky ground.

pages.text: Yellowstone is on top of a hot spot. Heat from Earth’s center warms up rocks and rainwater in the ground. Then hot water and steam move up and shoot out of the ground. The hot spot has also made hot pools of smelly mud and many colorful hot springs.
pages.brief: A cutaway view shows heat rising from deep underground, warming rocks and rainwater. Hot water and steam travel up through cracks and burst out as a geyser, while nearby a colorful hot spring and a bubbling mud pot release steam.

pages.text: Wildlife Many kinds of animals live in Yellowstone. The biggest animals in Yellowstone are bison. They can weigh up to 2,000 pounds (907 kg). Bison are hairy animals with a hump on their back. They roll in the dust to fight off flies and to get rid of their old fur.
pages.brief: A large, hairy bison with a hump on its back rolls in a dusty wallow, kicking up clouds of dirt. Flies buzz around it, and tufts of old fur cling to its shaggy coat as it rolls.

pages.text: The next-biggest animals are grizzly bears. They can weigh 800 pounds (363 kg) and are fast for their size. In the winter, grizzly bears sleep in dens under the ground for months.
pages.brief: A heavy grizzly bear runs fast across a meadow, then a cutaway shows another grizzly curled up asleep inside an underground den beneath the snow-covered ground, sleeping through the winter months.

pages.text: Settlers forced wolves out of Yellowstone over one hundred years ago. Later, workers for the national park brought them back. About one hundred wolves live in Yellowstone today.
pages.brief: A park worker opens a crate and releases wolves into a snowy valley. A pack of gray wolves trots across the grass, while in the background a faint scene shows settlers with wagons long ago.

pages.text: More than 350 other kinds of wild animals also live in the park. People may see elk, deer, golden eagles, fish, beavers, and foxes. Yellowstone is a safe place for them.
pages.brief: A lively Yellowstone scene shows an elk, a deer, a golden eagle flying overhead, fish swimming in a stream, a beaver near a lodge, and a fox. They share the safe, wild habitat of the park.

pages.text: History Native peoples hunted, fished, and gathered plants in Yellowstone. The geysers were also very important to their faith.
pages.brief: Native people gather plants, fish in a stream, and hunt with bows near steaming geysers. Their camp sits close to the hot springs, showing how important the geysers were to their faith and daily life.

pages.text: Later, European explorers went to Yellowstone. After taking it from Native peoples, the United States decided that no one could own or sell the land. The first national park was born.
pages.brief: European explorers in old-fashioned hats and coats stand before a steaming geyser, gazing at the strange landscape. Behind them, Native people watch from a distance as the explorers survey the land.

pages.text: There are now over fifty national parks in the United States. Some protect special natural areas. Others protect places that are important to remember.
pages.brief: A park ranger gestures toward a wide landscape that includes a forested mountain, a desert canyon, and a historic stone building. A group of visitors listens, learning about different national parks.

pages.text: Conclusion About three million people come from all over to visit Yellowstone every year. They fish, hike, camp, watch wildlife, and visit the hot springs. In Yellowstone, people can see natural beauty unlike anything else.
pages.brief: Many visitors enjoy Yellowstone: some fish in a river, others hike a trail, a family camps near a tent, people watch bison, and others view a steaming hot spring. The natural beauty stretches in every direction.

pages.text: Now that Yellowstone is protected as a it will always be around.
pages.brief: A peaceful Yellowstone landscape shows a geyser erupting, bison grazing, and a colorful hot spring under a bright sky. The protected park remains wild and beautiful, lasting for the future.

books.title: Sugar, Sugar, Everywhere
books.art_why: The book is about everyday foods, bodies, and health, all real-world subjects.

pages.text: Introduction What kind of sugary treats do you know of? Many people think of cookies and cakes. Sugar is in other foods, too.
pages.brief: Cookies and a slice of cake sit on a table beside a few other foods, showing that sugary treats are easy to name. The arrangement suggests that sugar can be in foods people do not think of as sweets. The scene is simple and bright.

pages.text: What Is Sugar? Did you know sugar is in milk? Sugar is also in plant foods. Fruits have sugar. Vegetables have sugar, too. The white stuff in a sugar bowl is table sugar. Table sugar is different than sugar from fruits and vegetables.
pages.brief: A sugar bowl filled with white table sugar sits beside a glass of milk, a piece of fruit, and some vegetables. The scene shows that sugar is in milk and plant foods, while table sugar looks different from the sugar in fruits and vegetables.

pages.text: When we eat sugar, our body changes it into a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose goes into our blood. It is a source of energy for the body. We need it to stay alive.
pages.brief: A simple view inside the body shows food being changed into glucose, shown as tiny bright dots in the blood. The glucose travels through red blood vessels toward the body’s cells, where it provides energy. The scene stays clean and easy for young readers to follow.

pages.text: Where Sugar Is Found The body can get all the glucose it needs from naturally sweet foods. Many foods from stores, though, have sugar added to them.
pages.brief: A table shows naturally sweet foods beside packaged foods from a store. The natural foods are whole and simple, while the store foods have added sugar. The scene compares where the body can get glucose and where extra sugar often comes from.

pages.text: Pasta sauce and ketchup often have added sugar. Many low-fat foods have added sugar. Sugar is often used to replace fat in low-fat foods.
pages.brief: A jar of pasta sauce and a bottle of ketchup stand beside low-fat foods on a kitchen counter. Small bowls show that sugar is often added to these foods, sometimes replacing fat in low-fat products. The scene focuses on everyday groceries with hidden added sugar.

pages.text: Breakfast cereal can have sugar, too. Many cereals have sugary treats added. Even cereals with plain flakes may have added sugar. How much sugar is in these breakfast cereals? 1 cup Grams of sugar Shredded Wheat 0g Toasted Oats 1g Corn Flakes 2g Crisp Rice 3g Raisin Bran 18g.
pages.brief: Several bowls of breakfast cereal sit on a table, including plain flakes, crisp rice, and raisin bran. A one-cup measure rests beside them, and the bowls show different cereal choices. The scene focuses on breakfast foods that may have added sugar, from plain flakes to raisin bran.

pages.text: Sugar and Health People need some sugar in their blood. It gives them the energy they need. But too much sugar in the blood can be bad. It can harm the body.
pages.brief: A person sits at a table with a steady snack, and a simple view of blood shows some sugar giving energy. Nearby, a much larger pile of sweet foods suggests too much sugar, which can be bad and harm the body. The mood is calm, not frightening.

pages.text: Over a long time, too much sugar in the blood can lead to problems with some parts of the body. The heart and other body parts might have to strain to work right. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A simple view of the heart and other body parts shows them working under strain, with tight lines around them. A person sits quietly nearby, and the scene suggests that too much sugar in the blood over a long time can make the heart and body work harder.

pages.text: Making Healthy Choices People can avoid some health problems by avoiding added sugar. They can eat more natural food. Sweet fruits have no added sugars.
pages.brief: A person holds a ripe peach beside a bowl of fresh berries, choosing natural food with no added sugar. The fruit looks sweet and appealing on a clean table. The scene shows that sweet fruits can be part of healthy choices without added sugars.

pages.text: They can eat more homemade meals. They can try to use foods that do not have added sugars.
pages.brief: A person prepares a homemade meal at a kitchen counter, with fresh ingredients spread out and simple bowls of food on the table. The meal is made at home and uses foods without added sugars, showing a practical way to eat more natural food.

pages.text: People can also try to limit sweet treats when snacking. They can reach for fresh fruit or nuts instead of donuts and cookies.
pages.brief: A hand reaches past a plate of donuts and cookies toward a bowl of fresh fruit and nuts. The snack table shows a choice between sweet treats and simpler snacks, with fruit and nuts close at hand. The scene encourages limiting sweet treats when snacking.

pages.text: Sugar makes food taste sweet. It can help keep our bodies going. Too much added sugar, though, can harm our health. Natural foods are a great source of energy. Fresh fruits and vegetables taste good and are good for the body!
pages.brief: Fresh fruits and vegetables are arranged beside a small bowl of sugar on a table. The natural foods look bright and appealing, while the sugar bowl sits apart. The scene shows that sugar can make food sweet, but natural foods are a great source of energy and good for the body.

books.title: The Grand Canyon
books.art_why: The book covers ancient peoples and 1800s exploration, so those events cannot be photographed.

pages.text: A Canyon So Grand The Grand Canyon, located in the Arizona desert, is so big that it can be seen from space.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Grand Canyon in the Arizona desert, a vast steep valley with layered rock walls. The canyon stretches so far across the land that it looks huge even from high above, showing why it can be seen from space.

pages.text: A canyon is a big, steep valley that is usually formed by a river. National Park The Grand Canyon covers about 1,900 square miles (4,921 sq km). In some places the canyon is more than a mile (1.6 km) deep. It can take two weeks to go through the canyon on a river raft.
pages.brief: A steep, deep valley cut by a river, with high rock walls. The Grand Canyon covers about 1,900 square miles and in places is more than a mile deep. A river raft moves through the canyon on a trip that can take two weeks.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon became a national park in 1919. National parks are special places. The land and the animals that live there are protected. Incredible Condors.
pages.brief: A protected national park landscape with canyon walls and native animals. A condor flies above the land. The Grand Canyon became a national park in 1919, and national parks are special places where the land and the animals that live there are protected.

pages.text: Formation Time and erosion helped form the Grand Canyon. Erosion happens when bits of the ground are worn away. For millions of years, the Colorado River ran over and wore away the earth until a canyon was made. The rocks at the bottom of the canyon are almost two billion years old.
pages.brief: The Colorado River flows over and wears away the earth, cutting deeper into the land over millions of years. Layers of rock form the canyon walls, and the oldest rocks at the bottom are almost two billion years old.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon is striped with colors. The stripes are layers of sediment that settled on top of each other over many years. Each layer helps us learn how Earth has changed over time.
pages.brief: The canyon walls show stripes of different colors. These stripes are layers of sediment that settled on top of each other over many years. Each layer is like a record that helps people learn how Earth has changed over time.

pages.text: Home in the Grand Canyon Exploration People have lived in the Grand Canyon for at least twelve thousand years. Native groups have hunted, built homes, and grown food there. The area is still home to many tribes.
pages.brief: Native people in the Grand Canyon area hunt, build homes, and grow food. They have lived there for at least twelve thousand years. The area is still home to many tribes today, and Native groups continue to live in the region.

pages.text: In the 1850s, settlers did not know much about the Grand Canyon. In 1869, John Wesley Powell led a trip through the canyon. Local people taught him about the canyon’s history. Powell and his team were the first to write the history down.
pages.brief: In the 1850s, settlers know little about the Grand Canyon. In 1869, John Wesley Powell leads a team on a trip through the canyon. Local people teach him about the canyon's history, and Powell and his team are the first to write it down.

pages.text: When the the canyon a national park, it forced local tribes to leave. They were kept out for a long time. Today, some Native people help protect the canyon and its history. A Tale of Two Rims.
pages.brief: When the Grand Canyon became a national park, local tribes were forced to leave and were kept out for a long time. Today, some Native people help protect the canyon and its history, keeping its story safe for others.

pages.text: Make Your Own Adventure Today, millions of people visit Grand Canyon National Park. Some hikers explore the canyon for weeks.
pages.brief: Millions of people visit Grand Canyon National Park today. Some hikers walk down into the canyon and explore it for weeks at a time, following trails through the huge landscape. The park is full of adventure for them.

pages.text: People like to raft on the Colorado River. It can be rough, fast, and rocky, making for a grand adventure.
pages.brief: People raft on the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon today. Rafts carry them along the rushing water between high canyon walls. The river can be rough, fast, and rocky, making for a grand adventure.

pages.text: People also love to walk on trails along the rim of the canyon. They can look out at miles of red and yellow walls and watch shadows move across the cliffs.
pages.brief: People walk on trails along the rim of the Grand Canyon. They look out at miles of red and yellow canyon walls and watch shadows move across the cliffs. The view stretches far across the land.

pages.text: A Natural Wonder The Grand Canyon is one of the most amazing sights in nature. Its land, peoples, animals, and history will be protected for years to come. Everyone who visits this national park is in for an adventure—and a view—unlike anything else.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Grand Canyon shows why it is one of the most amazing sights in nature. Its land, peoples, animals, and history are protected for years to come. Visitors come for an adventure and a view unlike anything else.

books.title: Russia
books.art_why: The book mixes modern Russia with czars, 1917 and the USSR, so drawings can show past and present together.

pages.text: Where Is It? Russia is a very big country. It is the largest country in the world— almost twice as big as the United States. Russia is part of both Europe and Asia.
pages.brief: A vast stretch of Russian land opens across Europe and Asia, with wide plains, dark forests and far mountains under a big sky. Beside it, a smaller patch of land shows how Russia is almost twice the size of the United States.

pages.text: Moscow is the capital of Russia. It is a big city in the European part of the country. More than twelve million people live there. The Russian president lives in a famous group of buildings in Moscow.
pages.brief: A busy Moscow street filled with crowds of people walking past tall city buildings. In the background stands a famous group of grand buildings where the Russian president lives, with towers and ornate walls under a cloudy sky.

pages.text: People Most people in Russia live and work in cities. The main language is Russian. In the country, jobs have to do with the land and the sea. For example, many people fish, mine oil and coal, and cut trees for wood.
pages.brief: In a city, people hurry to work past apartment blocks. Nearby, workers fish from a boat at sea, miners dig oil and coal from the ground, and others cut tall trees in a forest for wood.

pages.text: Sports such as soccer and ice hockey are popular in Russia. Russia is famous for music and a kind of dance show called ballet. Swan Lake is a famous Russian ballet.
pages.brief: Children kick a soccer ball on a grassy field while ice hockey players skate fast on a rink. On a theatre stage, ballet dancers in white costumes perform Swan Lake, with musicians playing in the orchestra pit below.

pages.text: Land The land in Russia is mainly low flatlands, high flatlands, and mountains. The deepest lake in the world, Lake Baikal, is in Russia. Russia has frozen flatlands in the north and wide grassy lands in the south. In between are huge forests.
pages.brief: A wide Russian landscape shows low flat plains, high flat plateaus and tall mountains. A deep blue lake, Lake Baikal, sits among them. Frozen ground stretches in the north, wide grassy land in the south, and huge forests fill the space between.

pages.text: Russia is a cold country, and it is home to the coldest village in the world. But many places in Russia also have beautiful summers.
pages.brief: A small village of wooden houses sits deep in snow under a grey sky, people wrapped in thick coats. Beside it, the same kind of village enjoys a beautiful summer day with green grass, flowers and warm sunshine.

pages.text: History In the past, czars, or emperors, ruled Russia. During that time, the peasants in Russia were unhappy. They didn’t like the way the czars ruled the people. They fought in 1917 to change their country’s ways.
pages.brief: A czar in rich robes and a tall crown stands before a grand palace, looking stern. Below him, poor peasants in simple clothes frown and look unhappy. A crowd of people raises their hands and fights to change the country in 1917.

pages.text: After the fight, Russia took control of a group of other nearby countries. Together they formed the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). The USSR had many problems, so it broke up in 1991. Today, Russia has a president.
pages.brief: A large group of nearby countries joins together under one government, with many people standing close. Then the union splits into separate parts as people turn away. Today, a president stands in front of a government building, leading Russia.

pages.text: Celebrations Many people celebrate Christmas and Easter in Russia. On Easter, they eat cakes and paint hard-boiled eggs. Russians also have a holiday to celebrate the end of winter. For this holiday, people eat pancakes with butter. They also have fun with sleigh rides and snowball fights.
pages.brief: Families celebrate Easter with sweet cakes and painted hard-boiled eggs on a table. Outside, people mark the end of winter by eating pancakes with butter, riding in a sleigh over snow, and throwing snowballs at each other.

pages.text: Food A popular soup in Russia is famous around the world. People make the soup from beets and other vegetables. Beets are red, so the soup also has a red color. Many Russians like a homemade drink. The drink has a sour flavor.
pages.brief: A cook lifts a spoon from a pot of bright red soup made from beets and other vegetables. A bowl of the red soup steams on the table. Beside it, a glass of homemade drink with a sour flavor waits to be tasted.

pages.text: Conclusion Russia is home to both crowded cities and wild forests. Russia has a long, rich history and many interesting things to do. The Russian people value the traditions of their beautiful homeland.
pages.brief: A busy city street packed with crowds and tall buildings stands on one side. On the other, a wild forest stretches green and quiet. Between them, people joyfully take part in a traditional celebration, showing they value the traditions of their homeland.

pages.text: Population: 142,423,773 Land: 16,377,742 sq km (6,323,500 sq. mi.) Capital City: Moscow Primary Language: Russian Name of Currency: ruble.
pages.brief: A wide view of Russia shows great crowds of people, huge stretches of land and the buildings of Moscow. A ruble coin and a ruble banknote rest in front, and people talk together in the Russian language.

books.title: South Korea
books.art_why: The book looks back at old kingdoms, 1905 and the Second World War, moments a real photograph of the scene cannot show.

pages.text: Where Is It? South Korea is a country in East Asia. It is close to China. The closest country to South Korea is North Korea.
pages.brief: A wide view of the green Korean peninsula, with South Korea in the south and North Korea touching it along the northern border. Across the water to the west lies the coast of China, and blue sea surrounds the land on three sides.

pages.text: The capital of South Korea is Seoul, the country’s largest city. Over nine million people live there. It is one of the largest cities in the world. Downtown Seoul has walls built more than six hundred years ago. The area contains many buildings from an earlier time.
pages.brief: A busy downtown Seoul street, tall modern towers rising behind an old stone wall more than six hundred years old. Crowds of people walk past traditional wooden buildings from an earlier time, with nine million city dwellers all around.

pages.text: People Many South Koreans speak Korean. Some people in Korea speak Chinese, Japanese, or English. South Koreans have many different types of jobs. They make cars, ships, and other things to sell in different countries. South Korea also has many computer jobs.
pages.brief: Inside a car factory, South Korean workers in overalls fit doors onto a finished car. Nearby, others weld a huge ship's hull and sit at computers in a bright office, speaking Korean as they make things to sell to other countries.

pages.text: Family is important to Korean people. South Koreans keep careful family records. School is important as well. Korean parents work hard to help their children learn.
pages.brief: At home, a mother and father sit with their child at a low table, helping with schoolwork, books open between them. On a shelf behind them a thick family record book keeps the names of grandparents and great-grandparents carefully written down.

pages.text: Land Most of South Korea has hills and mountains. The highest peak is Mount Halla, an old volcano, at 1,950 meters (6,398 ft.).
pages.brief: Rolling green hills and rocky mountain ridges stretch across most of South Korea. In the distance Mount Halla rises above the island of Jeju, its old volcanic top green and bare of snow, standing 1,950 metres high above the sea.

pages.text: Much of the coast of South Korea is broken up by rivers and streams. The land along the coast is very low. Most people in South Korea’s countryside live on the plains. Farmers there grow rice, fruits, and vegetables.
pages.brief: A flat green plain beside the coast, cut by a winding river and small streams running down to the sea. Farmers bend over flooded rice fields, and rows of fruit trees and vegetable plots spread out behind them under a wide sky.

pages.text: History For hundreds of years, Korea was a hard place to get to. Different kingdoms took control of the land. Japan took control of Korea in 1905, and did not give Korean people many freedoms. It remained under Japan’s control until the end of World War II.
pages.brief: An old Korean kingdom, with a king's palace and farmers working the land below the walls. In the foreground Japanese soldiers arrive in 1905 to take control, while Korean people watch, their freedoms taken away until the end of the Second World War.

pages.text: When the war ended, Korean people wanted to have their own government. The Soviet Union took control of North Korea. The United States supported South Korea. There was a war between the two sides. After the war South Korean people freely chose their leaders. North Korea had a leader put in place.
pages.brief: Korean people stand together choosing their own leaders after the war. To the north Soviet soldiers install a leader, to the south American support arrives. A line divides the two sides, and fighting has broken out between them across the land.

pages.text: Holidays The Korean New Year festival called Seollal is an important celebration. On this holiday, people celebrate becoming one year older. The Korean festival called Chuseok is another important holiday. Families visit family graves. They remember their family members.
pages.brief: A family gathers for Seollal, the Korean New Year, in traditional clothes, bowing to the grandparents, everyone one year older. Beside them another family walks to a grassy grave on Chuseok, standing quietly to remember the family members buried there.

pages.text: Food Korean food has lots of flavor. A vegetable dish called kimchi and rice are served at most meals. Many South Koreans think food is the answer to good health. They believe what they eat can keep them from getting sick.
pages.brief: A table set with bowls of rice and spicy red kimchi, a vegetable dish served at almost every Korean meal. A grandmother lifts a spoonful, smiling, sure that this food keeps her family healthy and strong.

pages.text: Conclusion South Koreans have shared the ideas of hard work and love of family for many years. Today, South Korea is a modern world power with a bright tomorrow.
pages.brief: A modern South Korean city at dusk, bright towers and busy streets full of people heading home to their families. Workers, parents and children move together through the crowd, hard-working and close, in a country looking forward to a bright tomorrow.

pages.text: Population: 51,715,162 Land: 99,720 sq km (38,502 sq. mi.) Capital City: Seoul Primary Language: Korean Primary Religions: Christianity, Buddhism Name of Currency: Won.
pages.brief: A wide view of Seoul, the capital city, crowded with millions of people. A Christian church steeple and a Buddhist temple roof stand among the buildings, Korean won coins and notes rest on a table, and green land runs out to the horizon.

books.title: All About Snakes
books.art_why: Snakes are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Some people do not like snakes. They may think snakes are gross or dangerous. Some can be dangerous. Snakes can also be beautiful and amazing.
pages.brief: A group of people stands back from a snake in a natural outdoor setting, some looking uneasy, while the snake rests in clear view; nearby, the snake’s body shows how a snake can look beautiful and amazing.

pages.text: Where Do Snakes Live? Many snakes live on land. Some snakes live in or near bodies of water. Snakes cannot live where it is cold all year long. Snakes do not live on some islands.
pages.brief: A snake moves across dry land beside a pond or stream, and another snake swims near the water’s edge; farther away, a cold snowy place where snakes cannot live all year and a small island with no snakes.

pages.text: Snake Traits Snakes are reptiles. All reptiles are cold-blooded and have a backbone. The body temperature of cold-blooded animals changes with their surroundings. They control their body temperature by moving to warmer or cooler places.
pages.brief: A snake lies on a warm rock in sunlight, then moves toward cool shade, showing a cold-blooded reptile whose body temperature changes with its surroundings; a close view shows its backbone and scales along its long body.

pages.text: Snakes that live in places with cold winters hibernate. They go underground or beneath things where the temperature stays the same. The snakes do not move until the temperature warms again. Snakes that live where it is warm all year do not hibernate.
pages.brief: Several snakes rest underground and beneath logs and rocks during a cold winter, staying still where the temperature stays the same; above them, snow covers the ground, and they do not move until warmth returns.

pages.text: Snakes do not have legs, and their bodies are covered with scales. They move by pushing their bodies against a surface. The scales help grip the surface.
pages.brief: A snake without legs pushes its long body against rough ground and a tree branch, its scales gripping the surface as it moves; a close view shows the overlapping scales covering its body all along.

pages.text: A snake’s skin does not grow with the snake. As a snake grows, its skin stretches and splits, showing new skin and scales beneath. The snake sheds its old skin and leaves it behind.
pages.brief: A snake rubs against a rough surface as its old skin stretches, splits, and peels away, revealing new skin and scales beneath; the shed skin lies left behind on the ground nearby, beside the snake.

pages.text: Most snakes lay eggs with soft shells. These snakes lay eggs where they can hatch safely. Other snakes carry their eggs in their bodies. The eggs hatch in their bodies, and the baby snakes come out!
pages.brief: One snake coils beside a hidden clutch of soft-shelled eggs in a safe spot, while another snake’s eggs hatch inside her body and baby snakes come out; the eggs and young are shown in a sheltered place.

pages.text: What Do Snakes Hunt, and How? All snakes eat other animals. Snakes use their tongues to find their prey. They stick out their tongues to “taste” the air. They follow the taste like a dog following a smell. Some snakes also have special body parts that can sense heat from other animals.
pages.brief: A snake sticks out its tongue to taste the air, following the scent toward prey; a close view of its head shows special body parts near its mouth that can sense heat from other animals.

pages.text: When snakes find their prey, some just bite and hold it. They may bite with their fangs or hold the prey in their jaws. Do Snakes Have Ears?
pages.brief: A snake bites and holds a prey animal with its fangs and jaws, not letting go; a close view shows its head and jaws holding the prey firmly in place while the prey stays caught in its mouth.

pages.text: Some snakes coil around prey and squeeze until it is dead. Some snakes have strong venom that they inject into prey through a bite. The venom may slow, stop, or even kill the other animal.
pages.brief: One snake coils tightly around a prey animal and squeezes until it is dead, while another snake bites and injects strong venom through its fangs; the venom can slow, stop, or even kill the other animal.

pages.text: Most snakes cannot chew. Instead, they swallow their meal whole. Some snakes’ jaws open so wide that they can swallow prey larger than their head! A Snake’s Meal.
pages.brief: A snake stretches its jaws very wide and swallows a whole prey animal larger than its head, since most snakes cannot chew; the meal goes down whole, with no biting or chewing into pieces at all.

pages.text: Conclusion Now that you know more about snakes, what do you think of them?
pages.brief: A snake rests in clear view in a natural setting, calm and detailed, as if inviting the viewer to think about what they have learned and to decide what they think of snakes after seeing many facts.

books.title: Migrating Geese
books.art_why: Migrating geese and the landscapes they travel through exist in the real world today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: When the days get shorter, the geese fly south. When the temperatures get colder, the geese fly south. When the leaves fall from the trees, the geese fly south.
pages.brief: A flock of geese flying south across an autumn sky, with shortened days, colder air, and leaves falling from trees below. The geese move together in the direction of warmer places as the season changes.

pages.text: The land will be covered with snow and ice. It is fall, and winter will soon arrive.
pages.brief: An autumn landscape of open land and trees, shown as winter approaches. Snow and ice are about to cover the ground, and the season is fall.

pages.text: The geese fly south in groups called flocks. They go to a warmer place. They take to the sky, and they get into formations shaped like the letter V. They head for a warmer place. They are migrating.
pages.brief: A flock of geese rising into the sky and forming a V shape. They fly together toward a warmer place, migrating as a group. The geese are high above the land in a clear formation.

pages.text: They can cut through the air like a knife. for the geese to move through the air. long distances. The V-formation makes it easier Flying in a V-formation helps the geese to fly.
pages.brief: Geese flying in a V formation cut through the air like a knife. The shape helps the flock move through the air over long distances, with each goose positioned behind the one ahead.

pages.text: The goose in the front of the formation has to work the hardest. The geese take turns flying in the front. When the goose in front gets tired, a goose from the back takes its place. This is how geese in a flock work together.
pages.brief: A flock of geese in a V formation, with one goose at the front working hardest. Another goose from the back moves up to take its place as the tired leader drops back, showing how the flock works together.

pages.text: It stays until the injured goose gets better. stays behind with the injured goose. and has to stay behind. Another goose Sometimes a goose in a flock gets injured.
pages.brief: Two geese on the ground, apart from the flying flock. One goose is injured and must stay behind, and another goose stays with it until it gets better.

pages.text: When the injured goose gets better, it continues to migrate. The other goose that stayed behind migrates, too.
pages.brief: The injured goose, now better, flies on to continue migrating. The goose that stayed behind flies too, and both rejoin the journey.

pages.text: If one goose needs help or is in danger, Geese are like a family. They take care of each other. other geese are there to help.
pages.brief: A group of geese together, caring for one another like a family. When one goose needs help or is in danger, other geese are nearby to help.

pages.text: The migrating geese find a warmer place. They find a place where lakes and rivers are not frozen. They find a place where the land is not covered with snow. They find a place where there is plenty of food to eat.
pages.brief: Migrating geese arrive at a warmer place with lakes and rivers that are not frozen. The land has no snow, and there is plenty of food to eat.

pages.text: They stay until the trees in the north temperatures in the north get warmer once again. get longer once again. They stay until the They stay until the days in the north begin to begin to leaf out and the grass begins to grow.
pages.brief: Geese in the north stay as days grow longer, temperatures warm, trees begin to leaf out, and grass starts to grow again.

pages.text: Once again it is time to migrate. But this time the geese fly north. It is spring.
pages.brief: Geese flying north in spring, once again on the move. The flock migrates back as the season changes.

pages.text: Food is plentiful, and spring has arrived. In the north, the snow and the ice have melted.
pages.brief: In the north, snow and ice have melted, spring has arrived, and food is plentiful for the geese.

pages.text: The geese mate and build a nest. The female lays eggs. Soon there will be baby geese.
pages.brief: A pair of geese mate and build a nest. The female lays eggs in the nest, and soon there will be baby geese.

pages.text: Soon it will be time to migrate again. Their parents will care for them and teach them to fly. The baby geese have hatched. They are called goslings.
pages.brief: Baby geese have hatched and are called goslings. Their parents care for them and teach them to fly, and soon it will be time to migrate again.

books.title: Extreme Insects
books.art_why: The book shows real insects and their natural traits, which can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Insects are always in danger. They have many enemies. They are food for each other as well as other animals.
pages.brief: Several insects face danger in a natural setting: other insects and larger animals threaten them, and some insects become food for one another and for other animals. The scene shows many small insects scattered among plants and ground, alert to enemies around them.

pages.text: Insects have many traits that help them stay alive. These traits include size, looks, and weapons. Let’s look at some of the extreme traits insects have that help them.
pages.brief: A group of insects shows different survival traits: one is especially large, one blends into its surroundings, and one displays a weapon-like body part. They are together in a natural habitat, showing how size, looks, and weapons can help them stay alive.

pages.text: Extreme Size This beetle can grow as long as a pen. It can weigh as much as a banana. Extreme size and a hard cover protect it from its enemies.
pages.brief: A large beetle with a hard cover rests near a pen and a banana, showing its extreme length and weight. It is in a natural setting, with the hard cover protecting it from enemies nearby. The beetle is shown as long as the pen and as heavy as the banana.

pages.text: This insect can grow longer than a new pencil. Its size frightens smaller insects away. Animals don’t eat it because they think it is just a big stick.
pages.brief: A long, stick-like insect stretches along a branch, longer than a new pencil. Its size frightens smaller insects away, and a larger animal nearby does not eat it, seeing only a big stick. The insect stays still among the branches.

pages.text: Extreme Look-Alikes Many insects look like other things. Their looks help them hide from animals that want to eat them.
pages.brief: Several insects look like other things in their habitat, helping them hide from animals that want to eat them. Some are disguised among plants while hungry animals search nearby, unable to spot them easily. The insects remain still and blend in.

pages.text: Some insects look like parts of plants. They can look like leaves, flowers, stems, or even thorns.
pages.brief: Insects are shown looking like parts of plants: one resembles a leaf, one a flower, one a stem, and one a thorn. They rest on plants in a natural setting, using these plant-like looks to hide. Each insect matches the shape of the plant part around it.

pages.text: There are insects with large fake eyes to scare hungry animals away. When scared, this caterpillar can make itself look like a snake.
pages.brief: A caterpillar with large fake eyes makes itself look like a snake when scared. A hungry animal nearby recoils from the frightening eyes and snake-like shape. The caterpillar is on a plant in a natural setting, using its look to scare the animal away.

pages.text: Extreme Weapons Some insects have extreme weapons to help them survive. Some of these insects use their weapons to get food. Others use their weapons to keep from becoming food.
pages.brief: Several insects with extreme weapons are shown in a natural habitat. One insect uses its weapon to get food, while another uses its weapon to keep from becoming food. Their sharp or dangerous body parts help them survive against enemies and prey.

pages.text: This insect digs a pit in the sand. It traps ants in the pit. Then it grabs an ant in its large, sharp jaws. Yummy!
pages.brief: An insect digs a pit in the sand and waits at the bottom. An ant is trapped in the pit, and the insect grabs the ant in its large, sharp jaws. The sandy pit is in a natural setting, with the ant unable to escape.

pages.text: This bug jumps on other insects. It stabs them with its sharp beak. It shoots out poison that turns their insides to goo. Then the bug sucks out the goo. Slurp!
pages.brief: A bug jumps onto another insect and stabs it with a sharp beak. It shoots out poison that turns the other insect's insides to goo, then sucks out the goo. The scene is in a natural setting, showing the bug feeding on its prey.

pages.text: Watch out! This beetle sprays out boiling hot poison when touched. It stops animals from trying to eat it.
pages.brief: A beetle sprays out boiling hot poison when touched, stopping animals from trying to eat it. An animal near the beetle is touched or startled by the spray and backs away. The beetle is in a natural setting, using its hot poison as a defense.

pages.text: Conclusion Insects have many ways to protect themselves. Their size, color, and weapons can help them stay alive.
pages.brief: Many insects are shown together in a natural setting, each using a different way to protect itself. Some rely on extreme size, some on color or camouflage, and some on weapons. Their size, color, and weapons help them stay alive among enemies.

books.title: Where We Get Energy
books.art_why: Real-world resources, vehicles, and power equipment can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction We use energy for many of the things we do every day. Energy lights, heats, and cools our homes and schools. Energy is part of everything we do. You need energy to run and play. You need energy to think and sleep. Where does this energy come from?
pages.brief: A warm home and a bright school show lights glowing and rooms being heated and cooled. A child runs and plays outside, then rests and sleeps in bed, showing that energy is used for everyday actions and rest.

pages.text: Energy comes from many kinds of important natural resources. Sunlight is our most important natural resource. Coal, natural gas, and oil are natural resources, too. So are things like plants, wind, and water.
pages.brief: Sunlight shines over a landscape with plants, a river, and wind moving the trees. Coal, natural gas, and oil appear as natural resources in the scene, while the Sun shines as the most important resource.

pages.text: Energy from Food Sources You get energy from foods you eat. Animals you eat may get energy from the plants they eat. Plants use energy from the Sun to make their own food. Plants can store the food they make in roots, stems, and leaves.
pages.brief: A child eats a meal at a table while farm animals nibble plants in a field. Nearby plants grow with roots, stems, and leaves in sunlight, storing the food they make in those parts. The sun shines.

pages.text: Energy from Gasoline Most cars, trucks, planes, and trains get energy from gasoline. Gasoline is made from oil. Oil is a natural resource found deep underground. Wells pump oil up from the ground. Factories change the oil into gasoline.
pages.brief: Cars, trucks, planes, and trains travel as a well pump draws oil up from deep underground. The factory stands nearby and changes the oil into gasoline, which fuels the vehicles. Oil is a natural resource.

pages.text: Electricity Electricity is a kind of energy. We use electricity to run many things that we use every day. How do we get electricity?
pages.brief: A bright home and classroom show lights glowing and several everyday machines running on electricity. A power line leads toward the buildings, showing one kind of energy people use each day. The rooms are busy.

pages.text: Making Electricity We can get electricity from a generator. A generator is a machine with huge blades that spin to make energy. A large power plant near your town may have many generators. Many kinds of fuel are used to run the generators.
pages.brief: A large power plant near a town contains several generators with huge spinning blades. Fuel is fed into the machines as they turn, making energy. The town sits close by, and many generators work together.

pages.text: Energy from Coal About half the energy used to run generators comes from burning coal. Coal is a natural rock resource that is usually mined under the ground. Power plants can burn coal to make energy to heat water. Burning coal also causes pollution.
pages.brief: Miners work in an underground coal mine, and coal rocks are loaded nearby. At a power plant, about half the energy for generators comes from burning coal to heat water, while dark smoke rises into the air. The burning coal causes pollution.

pages.text: When water gets hot enough, it turns to steam. Flowing steam makes the fan blades inside a steam generator spin fast. Generators use energy made by the spinning blades to make electricity.
pages.brief: When water gets hot enough, it turns to steam. The hot steam moves quickly past fan blades inside a steam generator and makes them spin fast. The spinning blades drive the generator to make electricity.

pages.text: Energy from Wind Wind can be used to make electricity. Blowing wind turns the large blades of a wind generator. The generator uses energy from the spinning blades to make electricity. Electricity from wind does not make any pollution.
pages.brief: A wind generator stands in an open field as strong wind turns its large blades. Inside the machine, the spinning blades make electricity, and no smoke or pollution rises into the clean air. The sky is clear and blue.

pages.text: Energy from Water Moving water can be used to make electricity. People build dams to block rivers. Water from a river moves through large pipes in the dam. The moving water spins the blades of the generators.
pages.brief: People have built a dam across a river. Water from the river flows through large pipes inside the dam and spins the blades of generators, making electricity. The dam holds back the river, and a wide river fills behind it.

pages.text: Energy from the Earth Some places under the earth are very hot. They have layers of hot rock and hot water deep underground. Hot steam rises out of holes in the ground. The steam is trapped in pipes and used to spin the blades of a generator.
pages.brief: Deep underground, layers of hot rock and hot water heat the earth. Hot steam rises from holes in the ground and is trapped in pipes, then used to spin the blades of a generator. The scene shows the hot layers below and the pipes above.

pages.text: Energy from the Sun People can use the Sun’s energy to make electricity. Solar cells and solar panels can into electricity. Solar cells make this car move!
pages.brief: Bright sunlight shines on solar panels on a roof and solar cells on a car. The panels and cells capture sunlight and turn it into electricity, and the solar cells make the car move along a sunny road.

pages.text: Switching Energy People use more energy each year. We use lots of coal, oil, and natural gas to run our cars, homes, and businesses. These natural resources can’t last forever, and they pollute the Earth.
pages.brief: A busy town shows cars, homes, and businesses using lots of energy, while piles of coal, oil, and natural gas tanks sit nearby. Dark smoke rises, showing pollution, and the resources look limited. More buildings spread outward.

pages.text: Sun and wind are good energy resources to use instead. They don’t pollute, and they last forever.
pages.brief: Bright sun shines over a field where wind turns tall wind generator blades. Green plants grow below. The clean energy scene has no smoke, showing that sun and wind do not pollute and can last forever.

books.title: Gorillas
books.art_why: Gorillas are living animals that can be photographed in African forests today.

pages.text: AFRICA.
pages.brief: A large black-haired gorilla sits among thick green leaves in an African forest, looking toward the viewer. Behind it, more forest trees fade into soft mist, and a younger gorilla rests on the ground nearby in the shade.

pages.text: Gorillas Gorillas are members of the great- ape family. They live in the forests of Africa. Some gorillas live high up in the mountains. Others live in lowlands.
pages.brief: Several gorillas move through a tall African forest, some climbing among leafy trees. In the distance, misty mountain slopes rise high above the trees, while in the foreground a lowland gorilla walks through ferns and low green plants on the forest floor.

pages.text: Gorillas have strong, heavy bodies. They are the largest primates in the world. Monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans are primates, too.
pages.brief: A heavy, strong-bodied gorilla stands squarely on the ground, its thick arms and broad chest visible. Nearby, a monkey sits on a branch, a chimpanzee grips a tree trunk, and a person stands to one side, all shown together as primates of different sizes.

pages.text: Gorillas can walk on two legs, as people do. Most of the time, they walk on their feet and hands. This type of walking is called knuckle-walking.
pages.brief: A gorilla walks upright on two legs across a clearing, then curls its fingers and walks on its knuckles with its feet and hands on the ground. A person walks on two legs in the background of the same forest clearing.

pages.text: Gorillas mostly eat leaves, stems, bark, fruits, flowers, and wood. Some gorillas also eat snails and insects such as ants and termites. Gorillas build nests in trees or sleep on the ground. They never sleep more than one night in the same nest. They travel to different areas in search of food.
pages.brief: A gorilla sits pulling leaves, stems and bark from a leafy branch, with fruit and flowers scattered on the ground beside it. Another gorilla presses a stick into an ant nest, and a nest of bent branches rests in a tree above.

pages.text: Gorilla Families A gorilla family is called a troop or band. A troop eats, sleeps, and plays together. Family members wrestle and play tag and catch for fun. They groom each other’s fur. Grooming is an important way for them to be close and friendly together.
pages.brief: A gorilla troop gathers in a sunny forest clearing. Two young gorillas wrestle and chase each other, one reaches out as if playing catch, and an adult sits calmly grooming the fur of another gorilla with its fingers.

pages.text: A gorilla baby nurses and stays close to its mother for a few years. It rides on her back to move around.
pages.brief: A mother gorilla sits on the forest floor holding her small baby close as it nurses. Later the baby clings to the thick fur of her back while she walks slowly forward on her knuckles through the green plants.

pages.text: When a male gorilla grows up, some of the fur on his back turns silver. The male is then called a silverback. The silverback’s job is to protect the troop.
pages.brief: A grown male gorilla stands facing the troop, the fur across his back shining silver. His large arms are braced on the ground and he watches the forest around the family group of females and young gorillas behind him.

pages.text: Gorillas Show How They Feel Sometimes, gorillas’ faces show how they feel. Their faces can show if they are happy, sad, or upset. Gorillas make crying sounds when they are upset. They make laughing sounds when they are tickled.
pages.brief: Close view of gorilla faces in the forest. One face looks calm and content, another looks sad and upset with a crying expression, and a young gorilla being tickled shows a wide open-mouthed laughing face while an adult's fingers touch its side.

pages.text: Gorillas have other ways to communicate. They whimper, scream, bark, and grunt. They even use smells to silently warn other gorillas of danger.
pages.brief: Two gorillas face each other in thick forest, one with its mouth open as it grunts or barks, the other whimpering. A third gorilla stands alert nearby, sniffing the air where a strong smell drifts between them.

pages.text: A woman named Francine taught a gorilla to use sign language. The gorilla’s name was Koko. Koko used signs to tell Francine what she wanted and how she felt.
pages.brief: A woman with light hair sits on the ground beside a black-haired gorilla in a leafy enclosure. Her hands are raised in a sign, and the gorilla's hand is lifted in a sign back toward her, both looking at each other.

pages.text: Gorilla Smarts Gorillas are very smart. They can make and use tools, but this doesn’t happen very often. A gorilla can use a twig to “fish” for ants. A gorilla can use a stick to check how deep a pool of water is. A gorilla can use a rock as a hammer to break open nuts.
pages.brief: A gorilla pushes a thin twig into an ant nest to fish out ants, then holds a long stick down into a pool of water. Beside a pile of nuts, another gorilla lifts a rock in its hand to break one open.

pages.text: Gorillas in Danger Many gorillas have been killed by hunters. Their forest homes are being cut down. Gorillas are now endangered. Many people are trying to save these great apes.
pages.brief: A gorilla sits on a tree stump in a forest where many trees have been cut down, leaving bare ground and fallen trunks. In the distance, people carry young trees and dig in the earth to plant new forest.
